title: Anthropic’s Nasdaq Journey Hits Major Roadblocks, CNBC Reports】
body:
The Nasdaq’s rally was abruptly halted this week as a series of cautious forecasts from the world’s biggest cloud providers sent technology shares tumbling, delivering the index its first three‑week losing streak since March. The downgrade, which centered on artificial‑intelligence‑driven workloads, has especially rattled investors in emerging AI firms such as Anthropic, whose anticipated public‑market debut now faces a far more uncertain path.

The turn began on Tuesday when Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud all revised their revenue outlooks for the quarter, citing slower-than‑expected uptake of generative‑AI services and heightened competition for enterprise spend. While each provider still expects double‑digit growth, the tempered guidance was enough to trigger a broader sell‑off in AI‑related equities. The Nasdaq Composite slipped 1.2% on the day, and the index has now logged three consecutive weeks of decline – a streak not seen since the market turbulence of early 2024.

Anthropic, the San Francisco‑based startup founded by former OpenAI researchers Dario Amodei and his brother, has been one of the most closely watched AI contenders since it secured a $4 billion investment round led by the same hyperscalers that now issued the cautionary notes. The company’s valuation, which peaked at $27 billion in early 2024, has been buoyed by expectations that it will soon list on the Nasdaq, potentially via a SPAC or a traditional IPO. However, the recent market sentiment shift has forced analysts to reassess the timing and pricing of any offering. “When the broader AI narrative weakens, investors become more risk‑averse, and that directly impacts the premium that a company like Anthropic could command,” said Maya Patel, a senior analyst at Greenleaf Securities.

The broader implications extend beyond a single firm. The AI boom, which has been driven largely by the promise of massive productivity gains and new revenue streams, is now confronting the reality of high infrastructure costs and a slower migration of legacy enterprises to cloud‑based AI solutions. Companies that bet heavily on AI hardware and software pipelines are seeing their profit margins squeezed, prompting a recalibration of capital‑allocation strategies. “The market is reminding us that hype does not equal sustainable earnings,” noted Thomas Liu, chief economist at the Financial Markets Institute. “Investors are now demanding clearer paths to profitability, not just headline‑grabbing product announcements.”

For Anthropic, the timing is especially critical. The startup’s flagship model, Claude, has been integrated into several enterprise platforms, yet it still lags behind the scale of offerings from OpenAI and Microsoft’s partnership. The company’s roadmap includes expanding its model size, improving safety features, and forging deeper integrations with the cloud providers that fund its growth. Yet each of those milestones requires substantial compute resources, which in turn depend on the very hyperscalers that have just signaled a more cautious spending outlook. This interdependence creates a feedback loop: weaker cloud forecasts depress AI stock valuations, which then pressure AI firms to delay or downsize their expansion plans.

Despite the short‑term headwinds, many observers believe the AI sector remains on a long‑term upward trajectory. The current slowdown may be viewed as a corrective phase that weeds out over‑optimistic projections and forces companies to focus on monetizable use cases. “We are likely seeing a market reset rather than a collapse,” argued Patel. “Companies that can demonstrate concrete ROI for their AI products will emerge stronger, and Anthropic’s emphasis on safety and alignment could become a differentiator as regulatory scrutiny intensifies.”

Looking ahead, the Nasdaq’s performance will hinge on whether the cloud giants can sustain their AI investments and whether enterprise adoption accelerates as promised. If the larger tech ecosystem regains confidence, Anthropic could still pursue a Nasdaq listing later this year, albeit at a more modest valuation than initially anticipated. Investors will be watching closely for any sign of renewed demand for AI services, as well as the company’s ability to translate its research into profitable, scalable products. In the meantime, the market’s cautious stance serves as a reminder that even the most promising technologies must navigate the fundamentals of revenue growth and profitability before they can secure a firm footing on the public markets.
